title: What they debate
hookLine: how revelation works, how binding halakha is, and how change happens

lines: A TREE, A STREAM, THE WALLS.
cards: An argument about an oven, in the Talmud. Rabbi Eliezer stands alone against the other sages. If I am right, he says, let this carob tree prove it, and the tree tears itself up and moves.
A tree proves nothing, they answer. Let the stream prove it, and the water flows backward. Let the walls of the study hall prove it, and the walls start to lean.
At last a voice from heaven: the law follows Eliezer. And Rabbi Joshua stands up and quotes Deuteronomy: it is not in heaven. The Talmud adds that God laughed and said, my children have defeated me.
Today: the questions under that story.

teach.b: What they debate. Three questions, and one under all three. First: how does revelation work?
The Mishnah draws a hard line here: among those it says lose their share in the world to come is the one who denies that the Torah is from heaven, in Hebrew Torah min ha-shamayim.

Some Jews hold that God gave the Torah, word for word, to Moses at Sinai. Some hold that God's revelation came through human beings, over time, with human hands and voices in it. Some hold views in between.
And they still read from the same kind of scroll on Shabbat morning.
Second: how binding is halakha, Jewish law? For some, the law is a command, as binding today as when it was given.
For others, it's a precious inheritance that guides but doesn't finally decide; a person weighs it with conscience and community.
Third: how does change happen? When the world changes, electricity, new medicine, new roles for women, who may adjust the practice, and how? A recognized scholar, ruling from earlier rulings?
A committee? Each community? Each person?
Now the question under all three: who gets to say?
The commandment, Deuteronomy says, "is not in heaven." It is near, in your mouth and in your heart. Some read it the way Rabbi Joshua did: the law now lives with its human interpreters.
Others read it as: it was given clearly, so it can be kept. The same verse holds both. Soon each movement gets its own day, in its own words.

how: The movements of modern Judaism differ mainly over how revelation works, how binding halakha is, and who may change practice and how; each answers these questions in its own literature and its own rabbinical bodies.

games.q: you're Rabbi Joshua. a tree, a stream and the walls have sided with Rabbi Eliezer, and now a voice from heaven does too. what do you say?
o: the voice has spoken; the law follows Eliezer.
let's ask for one more sign.
games.why: he quotes Deuteronomy: it is not in heaven. the Talmud says God laughed: my children have defeated me.

practice: Bring to mind one rule you live by, from a tradition, a parent, a teacher or your own conscience. Ask it the three questions gently: where did it come from, how binding is it for you, and who would get to change it?
Notice which one felt hardest, then let it go.
